families.name: Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (HRL)
families.definition: A method family that decomposes complex decision-making problems into a hierarchy of subtasks or skills to address scalability and sparse reward issues.

properties.text: HRL methods learn action selection policies at multiple levels of temporal abstraction to tackle long-horizon tasks.
These approaches often identify a small set of states as subgoals and learn corresponding skill policies to achieve them.
Architectures like FeUdal Networks decouple end-to-end learning across levels, allowing a Manager to set abstract goals for a Worker.
Some HRL methods use language as an abstraction to provide compositional structure for faster learning of temporally-extended behaviors.
HRL can be combined with symbolic planning to leverage prior domain knowledge and improve robustness in dynamic environments.
Regularized hierarchical policies serve as inductive biases for knowledge transfer across tasks in robotics.
Sub-policy adaptation allows skills to be continuously refined alongside the higher-level controller during new task training.

limitations.text: Training inefficiency often arises because the high-level goal space is large, making subgoal generation and low-level policy learning difficult.
Decoupling lower-level skill acquisition from higher-level control can lead to significant sub-optimality in transfer settings.
Acquiring effective yet general abstractions for hierarchical RL remains remarkably challenging.
Standard HRL methods may struggle with zero-shot generalization to unseen environments characterized by complex subtask dependencies.

families.name: Intrinsically Motivated Exploration
families.definition: A set of techniques that use internal signals, such as curiosity or learning progress, to drive exploration in environments with sparse or absent extrinsic rewards.

properties.text: Curiosity-driven learning enables organisms and agents to make discoveries to solve complex problems with rare or deceptive rewards.
Methods like DIAYN learn useful skills without a reward function by maximizing an information-theoretic objective using a maximum entropy policy.
Curiosity can be formulated as the error in an agent's ability to predict the consequence of its own actions in a learned feature space.
Intrinsically motivated meta-control arbitrates between model-based and model-free decisions based on the reliability of the learned model.
Self-supervised exploration via disagreement trains an ensemble of dynamics models to incentivize exploring states where model predictions differ.
These methods foster the exploration and discovery of a diversity of behavioral skills, ignoring local rewards to bootstrap learning.

limitations.text: It is currently unknown whether curiosity also helps to perform the hierarchical abstraction effectively.
Most formulations for efficient exploration are either stuck in environments with stochastic dynamics or too inefficient to scale to real robotics setups.
Intrinsic motivation may ignore rewards that are necessary for immediate survival or specific task completion if not properly balanced.

families.name: Event-Predictive Cognition and Segmentation
families.definition: Cognitive and computational models that segment continuous sensorimotor streams into discrete events to facilitate prediction, memory, and comprehension.

properties.text: Event-predictive encodings mirror interactions between agents and objects, supporting survival, tool use, and communication.
Hierarchical generative models 'reverse engineer' the intentions of other agents to comprehend sequential actions in real time.
Event segmentation theory proposes that clustering ongoing experience is adaptive for efficient online processing and later reconstruction.
Surprise-gated recurrent neural networks model the development of compact compressions of distinct event-like contexts.
Structured Event Memory (SEM) models combine symbolic scene representations with continuous vector spaces to account for event segmentation and generalization.
These abilities have evolved to distinguish food sources, produce tools, and cooperate, setting the stage for higher-level cognition.

limitations.text: The exact mechanisms of event segmentation remain elusive despite supporting behavioral evidence.
Compounding prediction errors in multi-step predictions can lead to performance degradation in model-based approaches.
Learning accurate models for complex dynamical systems is difficult, and models may not generalize well outside the distribution of trained states.

families.name: World Models and Latent Imagination
families.definition: Approaches that learn internal generative models of the environment to facilitate planning, policy evolution, and behavior derivation in latent spaces.

properties.text: World models represent knowledge about the environment to facilitate generalization from past experience.
Agents like Dreamer solve long-horizon tasks purely by latent imagination, backpropagating gradients through trajectories in the learned model.
Recurrent world models facilitate policy evolution by extracting features from compressed spatio-temporal representations.
Dual-system approaches combine model-based and model-free learning to improve sample efficiency in complex robotic tasks.
Dynamics-aware unsupervised discovery of skills combines model-based learning with model-free learning of primitives to make planning easier.

limitations.text: Dual-system approaches often fail to consider the reliability of the learned model when making multiple-step predictions.
Even accurate models for complex dynamical systems might not generalize well outside the distribution of states on which they were trained.
There are many potential ways for deriving behaviors from world models, making the selection of effective strategies non-trivial.

families.name: Symbolic and Neuro-Symbolic Integration
families.definition: Methods that integrate symbolic planning, logic, or structured representations with neural networks to enhance interpretability, reasoning, and data efficiency.

properties.text: Symbolic action planning resolves causal dependencies and breaks complex problems into sequences of simpler high-level actions.
Neuro-symbolic models like SEM embed symbolic scene representations in vector spaces to combine the advantages of structured and neural approaches.
Logic-Geometric Programming formulates physical reasoning and manipulation planning as an optimization problem integrating first-order logic.
SDRL introduces symbolic planning into deep reinforcement learning to handle high-dimensional sensory inputs while maintaining interpretability.
Abductive symbolic planning allows planners to deal with user-defined evaluation functions and prior domain knowledge.

limitations.text: Action planning is based on discrete high-level action and state spaces, whereas reinforcement learning is usually driven by continuous reward functions.
Symbolic planning relies on manually crafted symbolic knowledge, which may not be robust to domain uncertainties and changes.
Integrating discrete symbolic structures with continuous neural learning remains a challenge for robust decision-making.

families.name: Representation and Skill Discovery
families.definition: Techniques for learning abstract, low-dimensional state representations and task-agnostic skills that support transfer, composition, and efficient control.

properties.text: State representation learning focuses on features that are low-dimensional, evolve through time, and are influenced by agent actions.
Learning actionable representations aims for functionally salient features rather than just disentangled generative factors.
Task-agnostic policies can be composed to solve challenging transfer learning problems and unseen tasks.
Meta-learning approaches learn hierarchically structured policies with shared primitives to improve sample efficiency on unseen tasks.
Option discovery methods use proto-value functions to implicitly define options that traverse principal directions of the state space.

limitations.text: Most prior work on representation learning has focused on generative approaches, which may not capture functionally salient features for control.
Learning interpretable and transferable subpolicies from a single complex task is difficult without top-down decomposition or task distributions.
Standard deep reinforcement learning methods often suffer from poor sample efficiency because they aim to be entirely problem-agnostic.
The exact mechanisms of event segmentation in the brain remain elusive.
It is unknown whether curiosity-driven exploration effectively aids in performing hierarchical abstraction.
Acquiring effective yet general abstractions for hierarchical reinforcement learning is remarkably challenging.
Learning accurate models for complex dynamical systems is difficult, and generalization outside the training distribution is poor.
Integrating discrete symbolic planning with continuous reinforcement learning reward functions remains a technical challenge.
Most efficient exploration formulations are either inefficient for real robotics or fail in stochastic environments.
The extent to which non-human animals mentally represent problems and plan multiple steps ahead is far less clear than in humans.
There is a lack of approaches that successfully combine hierarchical abstraction with curiosity-driven exploration to overcome reward sparsity.
